claims.text: Ultrafast heating followed by rapid cooling kinetically freezes a disordered atomic arrangement into a single-phase noble-metal-based HEA nanoparticle.
Surface-energy differences and enthalpic interactions can drive segregation or phase separation if sufficient thermal evolution is allowed.
Plasma-gas-mediated modulation of cooling rate controls selection between a homogeneous solid solution and a segregated structure.
The initial material is a physical mixture of elemental noble-metal-based powders containing Pd and at least four additional elements.
Plasma gas composition should be varied while heating conditions and initial composition are held constant.
The applicable synthesis regime uses plasma temperatures above 5000 K.
The applicable cooling-rate range is 10^3 to 10^5 K s^-1.
Plasma gas composition modulates the thermal history of nanoparticles.
Cooling rate controls local atomic mixing by limiting diffusion and the ability of species to respond to miscibility gaps and surface-energy differences.
At extreme cooling rates, insufficient diffusion time prevents phase separation and freezes a metastable single-phase HEA.
Slower cooling provides enough atomic mobility for enthalpic and surface-energy differences to produce elemental segregation, phase separation, or heterostructuring.
Standard rapid-cooling conditions yield homogeneous, single-phase HEA nanoparticles.
Reducing the cooling rate will increase phase separation and elemental segregation relative to the rapid-cooled baseline.
Reducing the cooling rate will increase non-uniform particle morphology relative to the rapid-cooled baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies to nanoparticles around 50 nm in size.
The proposed mechanism applies to Pd-based or other noble-metal-based HEAs containing five or more elements.
Different phase-evolution behavior may occur outside the stated compositional and thermal-processing boundaries.
Individual diffusivities, trace impurities, and their responses to marginal cooling-rate changes remain uncertain because direct measurements at ultrafast timescales are limited.
Absence of a correlation between cooling rate and phase separation or segregation would falsify the cooling-rate-mediated kinetic-freezing hypothesis.
